items.title: Serve Robotics launches new business to become the AWS for robots | TechCrunch
items.summary:
Serve Robotics, a maker of self-driving sidewalk delivery robots, is expanding beyond its autonomous delivery operations in a bid to become a technology supplier to other companies building robots.

The company, which spun out of Uber’s acquisition of Postmates in 2021 and went public in 2024, said Thursday it will launch a new business line called Physical AI Services. [...] Specifically, Serve Robotics will offer customers its connectivity and data tools. Bedrock Robotics, a startup developing self-driving systems for construction equipment, is a customer, according to Serve. It’s also working with T-Mobile to bring AI computing power closer to robots, Serve announced alongside its third-quarter earnings on Thursday.

“We are solving the problem of robots in human spaces,” Serve Robotics CEO and co-founder Ai Kashani told TechCrunch. [...] Serve Robotics already makes two kinds of robots, the cute googly-eyed sidewalk delivery robot and one designed for hospitals that it got through its acquisition of Diligent Robotics.

Those businesses are not going away, Kashani emphasized in a recent interview. Instead, he said there is opportunity to sell the technology it developed for its own robots to other companies developing robots for farms, warehouses, and other uncontrolled environments.

items.title: Recent advances in AI are creating a 'paradigm shift' for robotics - Berkeley News
items.summary: Traditionally, engineers can directly program the software that tells robots how to perceive objects, plan movements and control their actions, a process called model-based robotics. Or, with model-free robotics, they can train robots to learn behaviors from demonstrations through imitation learning. The first approach requires extensive engineering, while the second needs enormous amounts of data and time. [...] Berkeley-based Ambi Robotics, which specializes in logistics and warehouse order fulfillment, applied the new methods earlier this year to analyze parcel sorting data and test updates to robot behavior. Tests showed an increased capacity of over 15,000 packages sorted annually per robot; the change is now deployed across 30% of the company’s U.S. fleet.

items.title: What will it take to integrate quantum computing into drug discovery? | Drug Discovery News
items.summary:
Quantum computing is often discussed alongside AI as another technology that could accelerate drug discovery. But while AI uses patterns in data to generate predictions and hypotheses, quantum computing takes a fundamentally different approach to processing information. [...] While classical computing relies on conventional bits, which represent information as either a zero or a one, quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, which can exist in multiple states at once. This makes them potentially well suited to simulating the behavior of electrons and their interactions – processes that underpin chemical reactions and molecular properties but can be challenging to capture using classical computational methods.

It's a completely new computing modality. [...] Quantum computing has the potential to accelerate and enhance drug discovery. But even as researchers work to improve the hardware and software, significant gaps remain in the infrastructure needed to bring the technology into biotechnology. Access to quantum computing remains difficult and expensive, while expertise spanning both quantum computing and biology is still limited.

We need people who understand each field and people who can work across both.

items.title: Chicago’s bid to lead the country in quantum computing | IBM Quantum Computing Blog
items.summary: The team at UChicago and IBM swapped in sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), a powerful quantum-centric supercomputing approach for solving chemistry problems, as the fragment solver. The resulting method, LASSQD, resembles LASSCF in important ways. It picks fragments, sends a circuit for each one to IBM quantum hardware, recombines the results, updates the orbitals classically, and repeats until the answer converges. [...] The region is also home to important quantum computing research. In 2026, a joint team from the University of Chicago and IBM demonstrated quantum advantage on a structured computational task, offering an alternative to traditional random circuit sampling benchmarks. Running on an IBM quantum system, the experiment leveraged 70 logical qubits to complete a calculation in approximately 15 minutes, surpassing the practical capabilities of today's leading classical simulation methods while [...] Following the announcement of the expanded collaboration in April 2026, the joint team delivered its first demonstration within six months: a computation of Cu₃C₆O₆, a strongly correlated kagome-lattice metal, using the integrated DeltaAI and IBM Quantum systems. The results will be presented at SC26 in November, highlighting the pace of innovation enabled by this collaboration.
